title: The Pollen-Season Runner
briefing: Sofia, 15, runs cross-country. In spring, walking through the park she sneezes a few times; on hard training runs through the same park her eyes stream and she sneezes in fits. On the gym treadmill, at the same fast pace, she doesn't sneeze at all.
question: Why does running harder make her sneezing worse — but not on a treadmill?

clues.title: Spring park, very high pollen
clues.text: The pollen count on her weather app says 'very high'. The trees along the trail are in full bloom.
clues.shows: lots of pollen in the air

clues.title: Streaming eyes, sneezing fits
clues.text: Itchy, watery eyes and bursts of five or six sneezes at a time. Her nose runs the whole way.
clues.shows: her immune system sounding the alarm

clues.title: Worse on hard runs
clues.text: On easy walks she sneezes a few times. On hard runs through the same park — breathing about 40 times a minute — she can't stop.
clues.shows: the harder she breathes, the more air (and pollen) she pulls in

clues.title: Treadmill: nothing
clues.text: Indoors on the treadmill at the same pace, windows closed, she breathes just as hard and doesn't sneeze once.
clues.shows: hard breathing only matters when there's pollen in the air

hypotheses.text: She's allergic to pollen; her immune system reacts to it.
hypotheses.flaw: Pollen alone doesn't explain why the same park is far worse when she runs hard than when she walks.

hypotheses.text: Hard running irritates her nose and airways.
hypotheses.flaw: On the treadmill she breathes just as hard and doesn't sneeze at all.

hypotheses.text: Both: her immune system treats pollen as an intruder, and running hard makes her breathe in far more air — so far more pollen — each minute, which sets off a bigger alarm.
She's catching a cold from the cold morning air.
hypotheses.flaw: A cold wouldn't vanish on an indoor treadmill or depend on the pollen count.

prediction.prompt: Sofia runs at a fast training pace. As the pollen count rises from none to very high, what happens to how often she sneezes?

second.question: At the same pollen count, if she slows from running to walking, what happens to her sneezing?

concepts.label: pollen in the air
concepts.hint: What's in the park air that isn't in the gym?

concepts.label: the immune system reacts
concepts.hint: Which body system is doing the sneezing?

concepts.label: breathing pulls air in
concepts.hint: What changes when she runs instead of walks?

concepts.label: a bigger dose
concepts.hint: How does running change how much pollen gets in?

concepts.label: no pollen, no problem
concepts.hint: What does the treadmill run prove?

transfer.context: Leo mows the lawn on a warm May afternoon and starts sneezing. Pushing the mower up the steep part of the yard, breathing hard, his sneezing gets much worse. Mowing the same lawn after a rainstorm, he barely sneezes.
options: Grass pollen sets off his immune system, and breathing harder pulls in more of it; rain washes pollen out of the air.
The steep part of the yard is colder.
He has a cold that comes and goes.
transfer.retryHint: Worse when breathing hard, almost nothing when the pollen is gone — which of Sofia's clues matched each part?
transfer.explanation: Leo's immune system reacts to grass pollen. Pushing uphill makes him breathe more air per minute, so he inhales a bigger pollen dose and the alarm gets louder. After rain there's little pollen in the air, so even hard breathing brings in little — just like Sofia's treadmill.

takeaway: The size of an allergy alarm depends on the dose. The immune system reacts to pollen; how much reaches it depends on how much is in the air and how much air you breathe. Run harder in pollen and you inhale a bigger dose.
